prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

By menopause, it’s not just estrogen my mother lacks. She’s lost her eldest son— that’s me, the one who’s queer—the doctor who once made her very proud. These days, I do my own wash when I’m home, I cook for her so she can take a break from all the chores she now refuses to assign to me. She sits, half-watching Ricki through her tea’s thin steam, her squint of disapproval more denial than it is disgust. She hears much better than she sees—it’s easier to keep out vision than it is to clear the air of sounds—and yet I know it’s age that stultifies her senses too. Enraged because she’s lost so much, I understand why suddenly she looks so stunned as from the television: “. . . Bitch, she stole my boyfriend, my own mother did! . . .” I fold a towel noiselessly. I know she thinks it’s garbage, sinful, crap—just as she thinks that taking estrogen in pills is not what God intended, no matter what the doctors say; or that I’m gay is plain unnatural, she can’t endure such pain. The oven timer rings. The cookies that I’ve baked are done. I’ll make another batch though she won’t touch them: given up for Lent. My mother’s love. I wonder where it went.

Keywords: She, These, Ricki

outputs.L1: By menopause, it is not merely estrogen my mother lacks. She has lost her eldest son—that is me, the one who is queer—the doctor who once made her so proud. These days, I do my own laundry when I am home; I cook for her so she might rest from the chores she now refuses to assign to me. She sits, half-watching Ricki through the thin steam of her tea, her disapproving squint more denial than disgust. She hears far better than she sees—it is easier to shut out sight than to silence sound—yet I know it is age that dulls her senses just the same. Enraged by all she has lost, I understand why she suddenly appears so stunned, as the television declares: “...Bitch, she stole my boyfriend—my own mother did!...” I fold a towel in silence. I know she considers it garbage, sinful, nonsense—just as she believes that taking estrogen in pill form defies what God intended, no matter what the doctors say; or that my being gay is simply unnatural, a pain she cannot bear. The oven timer sounds. The cookies I have baked are done. I will bake another batch, though she will not touch them—given up for Lent. My mother’s love. I wonder where it went.
outputs.L2: Menopause has taken more than just her hormones from my mother. She's also lost her firstborn son—me, the gay one—once her pride and joy as a physician. Nowadays, when I visit, I handle my own laundry and prepare meals for her, freeing her from tasks she now insists I not do. She sits before the television, tea steam rising between us, watching Ricki Lake with narrowed eyes that speak more of avoidance than actual revulsion. Her hearing remains sharp while her eyesight fades—perhaps it's simpler to shut out what she sees than silence what she hears—though I recognize both senses are dulling with the years. Understanding her frustration at all she's losing, I'm not surprised when a voice from the screen jolts her: "...that witch took my man, and she's my own mother!..." I fold a towel in silence. I know she'd call this trash, immoral, worthless—much like she views hormone pills as defying God's plan, regardless of what physicians recommend; or how she sees my sexuality as an unnatural burden too painful to accept. The timer buzzes—my cookies are ready. I'll bake another round anyway, though she's sworn off sweets for Lent and won't taste a single one. My mother's affection—I keep wondering what became of it.
outputs.L3:
# The Weight of Unspoken Things

My mother is losing her estrogen now, her body betraying her in the particular way that bodies do when they decide they are finished with certain chapters of themselves. But the hormones aren't the only loss she's grappling with—somewhere along the way, she also lost me, or at least the version of me she could point to with unambiguous pride. I am her eldest son, a doctor, a title that once meant something unassailable at family gatherings and church functions alike. Now I am also gay, and in her mind these two facts seem to cancel each other out, leaving her with a kind of grief that has no proper name.

I do the laundry now. I cook the meals she used to insist on preparing herself, back when doing so was one of the last domains she could fully control. She doesn't ask me to do these things—she simply lets them happen, a silence that speaks louder than any request could. It's a strange inversion of the roles we once had, and neither of us acknowledges it directly. We just move through the house, performing these small domestic tasks like actors who've forgotten they're allowed to speak their lines aloud.

In the evenings, she watches television with the particular intensity of someone avoiding a conversation. Her hearing has stayed sharp even as her eyesight fades, and I sometimes think this asymmetry mirrors something deeper in her—an ability to receive certain frequencies of reality while remaining conveniently blind to others. She hears everything I don't say. She simply chooses not to see the man standing in front of her, the one who loves who he loves, the one who exists outside the narrow frame she once had for him.

Her faith has given her a vocabulary for rejection that feels almost seamless, almost natural. Hormone replacement therapy, that clinical intervention meant to ease her body through its transition, strikes her as an affront to God's design—a refusal to accept the body He gave her. My sexuality registers in that same category, another unnatural deviation from some divine blueprint she believes she understands. In her mind, both are sins of interference, attempts to alter what should have been left alone. This conflation troubles me more than her disapproval alone ever could, because it means there's no separating her theology from her heartbreak—they've fused into something impenetrable.

And yet, I still bake her cookies. It's a small, almost embarrassing gesture in the face of everything else, but I keep doing it anyway. Lent arrives each year like a wall between us, another reason for her to decline what I offer, her Catholic discipline providing convenient cover for a refusal that runs deeper than any liturgical calendar. She won't eat them, of course. She rarely even acknowledges them beyond a cursory glance. But I bring them to her still, warm from the oven, because some part of me hasn't stopped hoping that one day she'll take a bite of something I've made with my own hands and, in that small act, take a bite of me too—accept me, however partially, however belatedly. It's a foolish hope, maybe. But it's the only kind I have left to offer her.
outputs.L4:
**Heat Index**

The television throws its blue light
across her face like a second, colder menopause—
some woman on the screen screaming about paternity,
a chair overturned, a studio audience
baying for more. My mother watches
with the sound turned up too loud,
the way she does everything now,
too loud or too silent, no in-between
since her body started its slow betrayal,
flashes of fire rising up through her like something
she can't confess to, sweat beading
at her hairline while she fans herself
with the folded church bulletin
still creased from Sunday, the one
with my name absent from the prayer list
though I am the one who brings her water,
who adjusts the thermostat three degrees
without being asked, who has learned
the exact temperature of her comfort
the way I once learned the layout
of my own hiding, folding myself
into smaller and smaller rooms.

She does not look at me when I hand her
the glass, condensation already forming
like the words we don't say. On the screen,
a woman is revealed to be sleeping
with her sister's husband, and my mother
clicks her tongue, says *disgusting*,
the word landing soft as ash
somewhere between us, and I wonder
if she means the show or means the shape
of my life, the man I might love
somewhere in a future she has already
closed the door on, quietly,
the way she closes doors now,
without slamming, just a soft click
that says more than shouting ever could.

I refill her water. I do not ask
if she's warm again, I only see it—
the way her hand goes to her chest,
the small fan she keeps by her chair
that she waves like something ceremonial,
like a woman blessing herself
in a language only her body understands.
I bring the fan closer. I say nothing
about the years, about the Wednesdays
I sat in her pew and prayed to be different,
about the silence she wore like a shawl
whenever I almost told her,
almost said the word that would have made
this room even colder than her own weather.

The talk show host asks his question
and the audience roars, hungry
for confession, for the small violence
of being known completely
and rejected anyway on television,
in front of strangers, at least
there is an audience for that kind of hurt.
Here there is only me, folding the throw blanket
over her knees though she hasn't asked,
noticing when her face flushes red
and reaching for the fan before she does,
this fluency in her body I've built
brick by brick, doing for her
what she will not do for me—
seeing me, truly, without flinching,
without the door closing softly
somewhere behind her eyes.

She thanks me without looking up.
The television laughs its canned laughter.
I sit beside her, close enough to feel
the heat rising off her skin,
far enough that we don't touch,
two people in the same weather
system, orbiting each other
in a house grown quiet with the things
we've agreed never to name,
the son who cares for her
like an animal caring for its wound,
instinctual, unrewarded,
continuing anyway
because the alternative
is a kind of leaving
neither of us can afford.
outputs.L5:
# A Morning with Ricki

She woke up early that morning, the sunlight streaming through her curtains in golden patterns. Ricki, her loyal dog, was already waiting by the bedroom door, tail wagging with anticipation for their daily walk.

She smiled as she reached for the leash hanging by the entrance. These moments—quiet, unhurried, filled with simple joy—had become the best part of her routine since adopting Ricki six months ago.

As they walked through the neighborhood park, she noticed how the trees had begun to change color. These autumn days brought a certain crispness to the air that both she and Ricki seemed to enjoy equally. Ricki would occasionally stop to sniff at fallen leaves, and she would wait patiently, in no rush to return home.

By the time they reached the pond, she sat down on a familiar bench while Ricki explored nearby. These small rituals—the walk, the pause by the water, the gentle companionship—reminded her why she'd wanted a dog in the first place. Life could be chaotic and unpredictable, but these moments with Ricki offered a steady rhythm she'd come to cherish.

As they headed back home, she felt grateful for the simple pleasures that filled her days, and for Ricki, who had become such an important part of her life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about a gay son caring for his aging, disapproving mother who is going through menopause, weaving in a trashy talk show like Ricki Lake playing in the background.
counterfactuals.output:
**Commercial Break**

The studio audience is screaming
at a woman who slept with her sister's husband,
and my mother fans herself with a church bulletin
from a funeral three weeks past,
her whole body a small weather system
turning against her.

*I told you, Ricki,* the woman on screen insists,
*I didn't know he was married,*
and my mother says *mm-hm* like she's heard
this particular lie before,
in this house, from someone else's mouth.

I bring her water with ice
the way she likes it, too much ice,
mostly water, and she doesn't look at me
when she takes it, just at the screen
where a man in a wig is throwing a chair.

*You'd think people would have some shame,*
she says, and I think of the years
she wouldn't say the word for what I am,
called it *that,* called it *this thing you're going through,*
as if I were the one sweating through my nightgown
at two a.m., as if I were the one
whose body had begun to speak
a language she no longer understood.

Now I am the one who understands the new language—
I know the signs, the flush that climbs her throat
like something rising to the surface of water,
the way she goes quiet mid-sentence,
fanning herself, furious at her own skin.

*It's hot in here,* she says, though it isn't,
and I get up without being asked
to turn the fan a few more degrees toward her chair,
the way I have learned to move
around the weather of her,
the way you learn a coastline
by the wrecks it's given you.

On television, a mother and daughter
are reunited after twenty years apart,
crying into a microphone held by a stranger,
and my own mother watches with her arms crossed,
unmoved, or moved in a way
she'll never show me,

and I sit beside her on the couch
that still has the smell of my father in it,
gone four years now,
and I think: this is a kind of love
that doesn't ask to be believed in.

I refill her water. I say nothing
about the years she wished me different.
I say nothing about the boy I loved in college
who she still calls *your friend.*

The commercial break ends.
Ricki comes back grinning, ready
for whatever's next, and my mother
leans forward like she might finally
find some answer in it—

how to be a body
that keeps betraying itself,
how to be loved
by someone she doesn't fully recognize,

and I hand her the fan
before she has to ask,
because some kindnesses
don't need to be understood
to be given.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poignant first-person poem exploring the strained relationship between a queer doctor and his estranged, hard-of-hearing mother, ending with a bittersweet image involving baked cookies.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Hands Remember**

I learned to read lips before I learned to read,
watching my mother's mouth shape *no* and *later*
and *not in this house*, her hearing aids
switched off like a door she could close
whenever my voice got too close to the truth.

Now I diagnose hearts for a living—
listen for the murmur, the missed beat,
the silence where a valve should sing.
I am fluent in stethoscopes, in the language
of what bodies won't say out loud.
I never learned hers.

She calls on Sundays, still,
asks about the *practice*, never the *practice of loving men*,
asks if I'm eating, if I'm cold,
as if warmth were the only thing
a mother needs to give.

I sign a little now—badly,
my hands stumbling like a resident's first sutures.
She watches my fingers like she's reading
an EKG she doesn't trust,
looking for the arrhythmia of *son* and *stranger*
beating in the same wrist.

Last visit, I found her in the kitchen,
flour ghosting her apron,
the oven's small sun warming the room
the way her voice never quite could.
She didn't hear me come in—
of course she didn't—
but she felt the floor shift,
turned, and there it was:
that old reflex of love
too shy to become a sentence.

She held out the tray. Chocolate chip,
my father's recipe, the one from before
he left and took the sound of easy laughter with him.
I took one. It was warm enough to burn
just slightly, the way forgiveness does
when it's finally offered—

not a cure, not an apology,
just sugar and butter and her hands
that made this small thing anyway,
that still know how to make something
for the son she doesn't
fully understand,

and I ate it standing in her kitchen,
tasting a peace neither of us
could say out loud,
the crumbs falling like everything
we still don't have words for—

only this: her cookies,
still warm,
still hers,
still, somehow, love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a narrative poem that uses a daytime talk show as a backdrop to reveal quiet family tension between a mother and her gay son, blending humor and sorrow?
counterfactuals.output:
**Channel 7, Two-Thirty**

The host wears a blazer the color of a bruise
healing wrong, and asks the boy on screen
if he's "always known," which makes the audience
lean forward like a held breath.

My mother mutes the commercial for a Roomba,
unmutes for the reveal.

*This is the good part,* she says,
though we both know she means
the part where she gets to watch someone else's son
instead of me, three feet away,
pretending to read the back of a Lean Cuisine box
I am not eating.

The studio audience gasps on cue—
a woman in the front row fans herself
with her own hand like she's at church,
like the Spirit just moved through Row C.

*Well I never,* my mother says, to no one,
to the television, to the space
just left of my head where she's been talking
for three years now, ever since I told her
in the Kroger parking lot, of all places,
because I couldn't wait
one more red light.

She spoons Cool Whip onto peach halves.
She says the mother in this episode—
the real one, the one crying in a folding chair—
is being *dramatic.*
*I'd never carry on like that,*
she says, meaning: *I already know how to grieve quietly.
I've had practice. I do it every Sunday
when you don't come to dinner.*

The host asks the mother on TV
if she still loves her son.
*Of course,* the woman says, wet-faced,
*I just don't understand it.*

My mother nods along like a metronome.
*That's exactly it,* she says.
*That's exactly the thing.*

I want to ask her: which part.
The loving. Or the not.

Instead I watch the credits roll
into a commercial for aspirin,
for the kind of headache
that comes from clenching your jaw
all day without noticing,

and my mother reaches for the remote,
finds the next show already starting—
another mother, another son,
another folding chair—
and settles in like it's a rerun
she can watch forever

as long as it's never
the one where she has to turn her head
three feet
to the left.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of an adult son doing chores for his mother, reflecting on her physical decline, religious disapproval of his sexuality, and the loss of her love, incorporating sensory details like tea steam and an oven timer.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Do With My Hands

I fill the kettle the way she taught me,
water loud against steel, and wait
for the small volcano of steam
to fog the window above her sink—
her handwriting still on the recipe cards,
her thumb-worn Bible on the counter,
open to something with my name
crossed out in the margins, though she'd say
she never wrote that. I know her hand.

I know the weight of it, too, unlifted
for the length of a hug in fourteen years.

The oven timer ticks like a small clock
counting down to nothing in particular—
casserole, her favorite, the one
I make because my hands remember
even when I've forgotten how to stay
in a room with her for longer
than it takes to reheat something.

She's smaller now. I noticed it
folding her laundry, how the sweaters
swallow her shoulders, how the cane
by the door has become a fourth thing
I have to remember to bring in
from the porch before rain.
I hold her arm crossing the kitchen
and she lets me, flesh loose
over the bird-bones I used to think
were permanent, the way I thought
her love was permanent, before I said
the true thing and watched it
leave the room like heat
through an open door in winter.

The timer goes off. I pull the dish out,
steam rising off it the same as the tea
steam rose an hour ago, the same
as her breath used to fog
the church-cold air when I was young
and she still reached for my hand
without thinking, without
scripture getting in between us
like a locked gate she now insists
was always there, was always
meant to keep some people out.

I set the table for two.
I fill her glass before my own.
This is what's left of loving her—
these small mechanics, the practiced
choreography of care
without the current under it,
the steam still rising, still
disappearing into air
that no longer holds
the shape of what we were.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary poem about generational and religious conflict between a mother and son, using irony (like Lenten sacrifice and Ricki Lake) to explore themes of rejection and quiet caregiving.
counterfactuals.output:
**Fish on Friday**

She gave up sugar in her coffee for Lent,
recited the rosary during commercials,
kept a Bible with gold-edged pages
on the TV stand, unopened, dusting
its cover with the same rag she used
for the ceramic Christ above the doorway—
his ribs showing, his eyes turned upward
toward a heaven she was saving a seat in.

I sat beside her on the plaid couch
those afternoons she called her sacrifice,
watching Ricki Lake instead of soaps,
some girl on screen confessing to her mother
*I like women* while the audience gasped
and clapped in the same breath,
a studio full of strangers more forgiving
than the woman passing me a bowl of soup.

She never asked. I never told.
We had an understanding built on silence,
thick as the incense at St. Anne's,
where she knelt each Sunday, praying
for my soul like it was a garden
gone to weeds, something worth
the labor of pulling, if only
I would let her hands get near enough.

Friday nights she made me fish sticks
from a box, said fasting was for sinners,
said it like a joke, but her eyes
went somewhere else—some other kitchen,
some other son she'd raised
to kneel on command. I ate in silence.
She watched me eat. That was the Mass
we said together: her offering, my body,
the blessing neither of us spoke aloud.

Now she calls at 8 p.m., asks if I've eaten,
if I'm taking my vitamins, if I've found
a church, and when I say no, she sighs
the sigh of women who've been sighing
since Eve took the apple and still,
somehow, got blamed for wanting.
I sigh back. It's the closest thing
we have to prayer.

Some nights I think of her alone,
saying rosaries to an audience of one,
offering up her only child
like Abraham on the mountain,
except no angel comes to stop her hand,
except I'm already here, already breathing,
waiting to see if she'll lower the knife
or if this too is just another Lent,
another forty days of going without
the very thing she means to save.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
